walkthroughs.body_html: 17000 plants globally produce 95 million m^3/day. Saudi Arabia largest producer. Sorek (Israel 2013) produces 627000 m^3/day, supplying 20 percent of Israeli household demand. Energy intensive: 3-4 kWh/m^3. Brine waste damages marine ecosystems; cost falling to $0.50/m^3.

$70 billion megaproject moves 25 km^3/yr from Yangtze to Beijing via 1432 km eastern + 1264 km central routes. Lifts water 100+ metres requiring pumping stations. Western route through Tibetan Plateau still unbuilt due to seismic risk and high cost.

Singapore strategy: local rain (catchment 67 percent of land), imported Johor water, NEWater recycled (40 percent of demand), desalination (30 percent). Tariff structure encourages efficiency. Population uses 141 L/person/day (UK 142, USA 310). Demonstrates demand management feasibility.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between physical and economic water scarcity?
options: Water scarcity only happens in dry countries.

Physical scarcity is insufficient water supply for demand (e.g. arid regions); economic scarcity is inability to access available water due to lack of infrastructure or investment, despite water being present.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
Economic scarcity means water is too expensive for governments to buy.
The combined loss of water from a surface through evaporation (from soil and water bodies) and transpiration (from plant leaves).
It is only water evaporating from puddles and lakes.
Economic scarcity means water is too expensive for governments to buy.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.

mcqs.q: What are the four pillars of food security?
options: Economic scarcity means water is too expensive for governments to buy.
Availability (enough food exists), access (people can obtain it), utilisation (nutritional quality and absorption) and stability (consistent over time) — defined by the FAO.
Food security means storing food for emergencies.
Food security just means producing enough food.
